editorial.headline: The Used-Electronics Trade Bali’s PMA Moratorium Stops
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, but a Bali-wide PMA moratorium blocks registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
A business under this activity trades in used electrical and electronic goods at retail: second-hand radios, tape recorders, televisions, washing machines, electric irons, and hair dryers or curlers. Nationally, it is open to foreign investment, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In Bali, however, the practical answer is unequivocal: a foreign investor cannot register this activity for PMA today. The activity is blocked by Bali’s moratorium on PMA registration for Low and Medium-Low risk activities, applied island-wide on a permanent basis.

The character of the business matters. This is not a general description of electronics retail, but a defined trade in previously used electrical and electronic items. The examples give the category its useful commercial shape: household appliances sit alongside consumer audio and television equipment, while personal-care electrical goods are also expressly within scope. It is therefore an activity grounded in the resale of used equipment, rather than the manufacture, repair, or unspecified distribution of those goods.

The registration is open across the full stated range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That broad national availability does not soften the Bali result for PMA. The Bali classification records that, at the Besar scale, every scope carries a Low or Medium-Low risk assessment. That is the condition that brings the activity within the provincial moratorium. The national position and the Bali position are consequently not competing descriptions of the same outcome; they operate at different levels. Nationally, foreign ownership may reach 100%. In Bali, PMA registration is blocked.

For founders, the important discipline is to keep those two truths in view at once. The national foreign-investment setting signals that this used-electronics retail activity is open in principle. Bali’s province-wide rule then determines that the activity cannot be registered there as PMA because of its risk classification. That is not a marginal qualification to be discovered after choosing a scale or assembling a product range; it is the central local constraint. A business plan built around the retail resale of used electrical and electronic goods must treat Bali’s PMA block as decisive from the outset.
